html:
Current Electricity and Magnetism is the third-heaviest area of the Physics paper: 9 of the 50 questions, with about 3 questions from this chapter.

The marks are unusually predictable — a resistance or power calculation, a two-loop Kirchhoff network, a metre-bridge or potentiometer reading, a galvanometer conversion, and one fact about the thermocouple.

Almost every question is a formula applied once, so the chapter rewards precision rather than insight: the right formula, the right units, the right sign.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • I = nAev_d, R = \rho L/A, and how \rho changes with temperature (positive for metals, negative for semiconductors).
  • emf against terminal pd: V = E - Ir; the V–I graph has intercept E and slope -r.
  • P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R; H = I^2Rt; 1 kWh = 3.6\times10^6 J and the electricity bill.
  • Series and parallel rules; cells in series, in parallel and in mixed rows.
  • Kirchhoff's two laws on a two-loop network, with consistent signs.
  • Wheatstone balance P/Q = R/S; metre bridge R/S = l/(100-l); potentiometer E \propto l.
  • Shunt S = I_gG/(I-I_g) for an ammeter; multiplier R = V/I_g - G for a voltmeter.
  • Seebeck and Peltier effects; neutral temperature \theta_n and inversion temperature \theta_i = 2\theta_n - \theta_c.

14.1 Ohm's law and Joule's law; resistance, resistivity, emf, potential difference, energy and power

14.1.1 Electric current, drift velocity and current density

Electric current is the rate of flow of charge through a cross-section: I = Q/t, measured in amperes (1 A = 1 C s⁻¹). By convention the direction of current is the direction in which positive charge would flow, opposite to the motion of the electrons in a metal.

The electrons do not travel along the wire at the speed of the current. They move at a slow drift velocity v_d (typically 10^{-4} m s⁻¹, a fraction of a millimetre per second) superimposed on a much faster random motion.

The lamp lights the instant you close the switch because the electric field is set up along the wire at nearly the speed of light, and every electron starts drifting almost at once.

If a conductor has n free electrons per unit volume, cross-section A, and drift velocity v_d, then in time t the charge crossing a section is neAv_dt, so

I = nAev_d \qquad\text{and}\qquad J = \frac{I}{A} = nev_d

J is the current density, a vector, measured in A m⁻². Current itself is a scalar: it has a sense of flow but adds algebraically at a junction.

Why the drift is slow but steady. The field accelerates each electron, but collisions with the vibrating lattice randomise the motion. The average time between collisions is the relaxation time \tau, and the drift speed settles at

v_d = \frac{eE\tau}{m}

so the mobility is \mu = v_d/E = e\tau/m.

14.1.2 Ohm's law

Ohm's law

At constant temperature, the current through a metallic conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it: V = IR, where R is the resistance in ohms (Ω).

The law is not universal. It holds for metals at constant temperature, but fails for a filament lamp (whose temperature rises), for a diode, for electrolytes and for thermistors. Those are called non-ohmic conductors, and their I–V graphs are curved.

Graph Shape for an ohmic conductor What the slope gives
V against I straight line through the origin resistance R
I against V straight line through the origin conductance 1/R

Resistance R = V/I depends on the material, the length, the cross-section and the temperature. Conductance G = 1/R is measured in siemens (S).

14.1.3 Resistivity

For a uniform conductor of length L and cross-section A,

R = \frac{\rho L}{A}

where \rho is the resistivity (or specific resistance), a property of the material alone, measured in Ω m. Resistivity does not change when a wire is cut, stretched or bent; the resistance does.

Resistivity from the free-electron model

Setting up. A wire of length L, area A, carrying current I under a field E = V/L.

Step 1 — current in terms of drift speed. I = nAev_d.

Step 2 — drift speed in terms of the field. v_d = eE\tau/m.

Step 3 — substitute and put E = V/L.

I = nAe\frac{e\tau}{m}\frac{V}{L} = \frac{ne^2A\tau}{mL}\,V

Step 4 — compare with V = IR and R = \rho L/A.

R = \frac{mL}{ne^2A\tau} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \rho = \frac{m}{ne^2\tau}

Result. \rho = m/(ne^2\tau) and \sigma = 1/\rho = ne^2\tau/m.

What it means. Resistivity is high when there are few carriers (n small) or short collisions (\tau small). In a metal, heating increases the lattice vibration, shortens \tau, and so raises \rho.

Material (approximate, at room temperature) \rho / Ω m Class
Silver 1.6\times10^{-8} conductor
Copper 1.7\times10^{-8} conductor
Aluminium 2.8\times10^{-8} conductor
Nichrome 1.0\times10^{-6} alloy, heating element
Manganin, constantan \approx 5\times10^{-7} alloy, standard resistor
Germanium \approx 0.6 semiconductor
Glass 10^{10}–10^{14} insulator
Shape changes resistance, not resistivity

A wire stretched to twice its length (volume unchanged) has half the area, so R = \rho L/A becomes 4R — the resistance goes up four times, while \rho is unchanged. Cut into n equal parts, each part has R/n; joined all in parallel they give R/n^2.

14.1.4 How resistance changes with temperature

R_t = R_0(1 + \alpha\,\Delta t) \qquad\text{and}\qquad \alpha = \frac{1}{R_0}\frac{dR}{dt}

where \alpha is the temperature coefficient of resistance, in K⁻¹.

Material Sign of \alpha Reason
Metals (Cu, Al, W) positive, about 4\times10^{-3} K⁻¹ heating shortens \tau; \rho = m/(ne^2\tau) rises
Alloys (manganin, constantan, nichrome) almost zero used for standard resistors and shunts
Semiconductors (Ge, Si), carbon negative heating frees many more carriers, so n rises faster than \tau falls

Because manganin's resistance barely changes with temperature, it is wound into standard resistance coils, shunts and the wire of a potentiometer.

14.1.5 emf, potential difference and internal resistance

The electromotive force (emf) E of a source is the work done by the source in carrying unit positive charge round the complete circuit. It is measured in volts but it is not a force.

The potential difference between two points is the work done per unit charge in carrying charge between those points through the external circuit.

A real cell has an internal resistance r, so part of its emf is spent inside the cell:

V = E - Ir \qquad\text{with}\qquad V = IR \quad\text{and}\quad I = \frac{E}{R+r}

Situation Terminal pd
Open circuit (I = 0) V = E
Discharging through R V = E - Ir, always less than E
Being charged by a stronger source V = E + Ir, greater than E
Short circuit (R = 0) V = 0, I = E/r (the largest possible current)

Rearranging gives the internal resistance from two measurements:

r = \frac{E - V}{I} = R\left(\frac{E}{V} - 1\right)

Maximum power transfer. The power delivered to the external resistor is P = I^2R = E^2R/(R+r)^2, which is greatest when R = r. Then P_{max} = E^2/(4r), the terminal voltage is E/2, and the efficiency is only 50 % — half the energy is wasted inside the cell.

14.1.6 Joule's law, power and the electricity bill

When current flows through a resistance, the electrical energy is converted into heat. Joule's law:

H = I^2Rt = VIt = \frac{V^2 t}{R}

and the power (energy per second) is

P = VI = I^2R = \frac{V^2}{R}

Quantity Unit Note
Energy joule (J) 1 J = 1 W s
Power watt (W) 1 kW = 1000 W
Commercial unit kilowatt-hour (kWh) 1 kWh = 3.6\times10^6 J = 1 "unit"

The electricity meter measures energy, not power. A 100 W lamp left on for 10 h uses 1 kWh — one unit.

Worked example 14.1 — an NEA bill

Problem. A 1500 W water heater runs 4 hours a day for 30 days. If NEA charges Rs 11 per unit, what is the cost?

Solution. Energy = 1.5\ \text{kW}\times4\ \text{h}\times30 = 180 kWh = 180 units. Cost = 180\times11 = Rs 1980. In joules the same energy is 180\times3.6\times10^6 = 6.48\times10^8 J.

Two bulbs in series: the dim one wins

A 60 W and a 100 W bulb are both rated for 220 V. Their resistances are R = V^2/P, so the 60 W bulb has the larger resistance. In series the same current passes through both, and P = I^2R makes the 60 W bulb glow brighter.

In parallel, each gets the full 220 V and the 100 W bulb is brighter. Never assume the higher-wattage bulb is always the brighter one.

Power formulas: choose by what is constant

In series the current is common, so use P = I^2R (power \propto R). In parallel the voltage is common, so use P = V^2/R (power \propto 1/R). This one choice settles almost every "which bulb is brighter" question.

14.2 Resistors in series and parallel; Kirchhoff's laws

14.2.1 Series and parallel combinations

Series Parallel
Connection end to end all left ends joined, all right ends joined
Same through each current potential difference
Adds voltages: V = V_1 + V_2 + \dots currents: I = I_1 + I_2 + \dots
Equivalent R_s = R_1 + R_2 + \dots \frac{1}{R_p} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \dots
Two resistors R_1 + R_2 \frac{R_1R_2}{R_1+R_2} (product over sum)
n equal resistors nR R/n
Result larger than the biggest smaller than the smallest

Current division between two parallel resistors: I_1 = I\dfrac{R_2}{R_1+R_2} — the larger share goes through the smaller resistance.

Adding a parallel path always lowers the resistance

Adding any resistor in parallel gives the current another route, so the equivalent resistance falls — it can never rise. A common distractor offers "increases because another resistor is added".

14.2.2 Cells in series and in parallel

Arrangement Current through R Best when
n cells in series (aiding) I = \dfrac{nE}{R + nr} R \gg r
n cells in parallel I = \dfrac{E}{R + r/n} R \ll r
m rows of n cells (mixed) I = \dfrac{nE}{R + nr/m} R = nr/m gives the maximum

In the mixed grouping the current is greatest when the external resistance equals the total internal resistance of the battery, R = nr/m. Series connection raises the emf; parallel connection lowers the internal resistance; mixed grouping does both.

Series cells must aid each other

If one cell is reversed, the total emf becomes (n-2)E, not nE. Read the polarity in the diagram before adding emfs.

Worked example 14.2 — mixed grouping

Problem. Eight cells, each of emf 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω, are joined in 2 rows of 4 and connected to a 1 Ω resistor. Find the current.

Solution. Here n = 4, m = 2:

I = \frac{nE}{R + nr/m} = \frac{4(1.5)}{1 + 4(0.5)/2} = \frac{6}{1+1} = 3\ \text{A}

All eight in series the current would be 12/(1+4) = 2.4 A; all eight in parallel, 1.5/(1+0.5/8) \approx 1.4 A. The mixed arrangement beats both because it raises the emf and lowers the internal resistance at the same time.

14.2.3 Kirchhoff's laws

Kirchhoff's laws

Junction rule. The sum of the currents entering a junction equals the sum of the currents leaving it — conservation of charge. Loop rule. The algebraic sum of the potential changes round any closed loop is zero — conservation of energy.

Sign convention (fix it once and keep it):

Move Change
Across a resistor with the current -IR
Across a resistor against the current +IR
Across a cell from - to + +E
Across a cell from + to - -E

Worked example 14.3 — the two-loop network

Problem. In the figure, E_1 = 12 V with r_1 = 1\ \Omega; E_2 = 6 V with r_2 = 1\ \Omega; the middle resistor is R = 4\ \Omega. Find the current in each branch.

Solution. Take I_1 upward in the left branch, I_2 upward in the right branch, and I_3 downward through R.

Junction A: I_3 = I_1 + I_2.

Left loop (through R, then the 12 V cell):

-4I_3 - 1\cdot I_1 + 12 = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 4I_3 + I_1 = 12

Right loop:

-4I_3 - 1\cdot I_2 + 6 = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 4I_3 + I_2 = 6

Substituting I_3: 5I_1 + 4I_2 = 12 and 4I_1 + 5I_2 = 6. Subtracting gives I_1 - I_2 = 6, and then I_2 = -2 A, I_1 = 4 A, I_3 = 2 A.

Reading the signs. The minus sign on I_2 means the current in the right branch actually flows downward: the 12 V cell forces 2 A backwards through the 6 V cell, so the 6 V cell is being charged. The pd across R is I_3R = 8 V.

Power check. Supplied: 12\times4 = 48 W. Used: 4^2(1) = 16 W in r_1, 2^2(1) = 4 W in r_2, 2^2(4) = 16 W in R, and 6\times2 = 12 W charging the 6 V cell. Total 48 W. ✓

Which method to use

For a network with one unknown, use series–parallel reduction. For two or more unknowns, label the currents and write one junction equation plus one loop equation per independent loop. Always finish by checking the power balance — it catches a sign error in seconds.

14.3 Wheatstone bridge, metre bridge and potentiometer; a galvanometer converted to an ammeter and a voltmeter

14.3.1 The Wheatstone bridge

Four resistances P, Q, R, S form a quadrilateral ABCD; a galvanometer joins B to D and a cell joins A to C. The bridge is balanced when the galvanometer shows no deflection:

\frac{P}{Q} = \frac{R}{S}

Balance condition of the Wheatstone bridge

Setting up. At balance the galvanometer carries no current, so B and D are at the same potential.

Step 1 — no current through the galvanometer means the current I_1 through P continues through Q, and the current I_2 through R continues through S.

Step 2 — equal potentials at B and D.

V_A - V_B = V_A - V_D \qquad\text{and}\qquad V_B - V_C = V_D - V_C

Step 3 — write each drop as IR.

I_1P = I_2R \qquad\text{and}\qquad I_1Q = I_2S

Step 4 — divide the first equation by the second.

\frac{P}{Q} = \frac{R}{S}

Result. The bridge balances when the ratio of the two resistances on one side equals the ratio on the other.

What it means. At balance no current flows through the galvanometer, so the measurement does not disturb the network.

The condition contains only ratios, so it is unaffected by the emf of the cell, and interchanging the cell and the galvanometer leaves it unchanged. The bridge is most sensitive when all four resistances are of the same order.

14.3.2 The metre bridge

The metre bridge is a practical Wheatstone bridge.

A one-metre uniform wire AC carries the two ratio arms as lengths: the unknown resistance R is in the left gap, a known resistance S in the right gap, and a jockey slides along the wire to find the balance point at length l from A.

Since the resistance of a uniform wire is proportional to its length, the two lower arms have resistances in the ratio l : (100-l), so

\frac{R}{S} = \frac{l}{100-l} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad R = S\,\frac{l}{100-l}

Metre bridge pitfalls
  • The balance point should be near the middle of the wire; there the bridge is most sensitive. A balance point at 5 cm or 95 cm gives a poor measurement, and the remedy is to change S.
  • The wire must be uniform and the contacts clean; end corrections allow for the resistance of the copper strips at the ends.
  • The jockey must be tapped, not dragged, or the wire is scraped and its cross-section changes.
Worked example 14.4 — metre bridge

Problem. With a 6 Ω resistor in the right gap, the balance point is 40 cm from the left end. Find the resistance in the left gap.

Solution. R = S\dfrac{l}{100-l} = 6\times\dfrac{40}{60} = 4\ \Omega. The unknown is smaller than the standard, so its balance length is the shorter one — a quick check on the answer.

14.3.3 The potentiometer

A steady current from a driver cell flows through a long uniform wire AB, giving a constant potential gradient k = V_{AB}/L (V m⁻¹).

The cell whose emf is to be measured is connected between A and a jockey, with a galvanometer in series. The jockey is moved until the galvanometer shows no deflection; then the pd across the balanced length l equals the emf:

E = kl \qquad\text{so}\qquad E \propto l

Comparing two emfs. With the same potential gradient, E_1/E_2 = l_1/l_2 — no need to know k at all.

Measuring internal resistance. First balance the cell on open circuit (length l_1), giving E = kl_1. Then connect a known resistance R across the cell and balance again (length l_2), giving V = kl_2. Since V = ER/(R+r),

r = R\left(\frac{l_1}{l_2} - 1\right)

Why a potentiometer measures emf and a voltmeter does not

At the balance point the galvanometer carries no current, so no current is drawn from the cell being tested. With I = 0 there is no drop Ir inside the cell, and the pd across the wire equals the cell's full emf.

A voltmeter must draw some current to move its pointer, so it always reads V = E - Ir, slightly less than the emf. This is why the potentiometer is a null method and is more accurate.

Advantage of the potentiometer Reason
Measures emf, not terminal pd no current is drawn at balance
Very small emfs measurable potential gradient can be made small (long wire, low V)
No calibration drift of a meter it is a ratio of lengths
Internal resistance measurable two balance readings, with and without R

Sensitivity rises when the potential gradient is made smaller — a longer wire, or a smaller current through it.

14.3.4 Converting a galvanometer into an ammeter and a voltmeter

A galvanometer deflects full scale for a small current I_g and has a coil resistance G. To use it as an ammeter or a voltmeter it must be adapted.

As an ammeter — a low resistance (shunt) in parallel. The shunt carries the excess current:

S = \frac{I_gG}{I - I_g}, \qquad R_A = \frac{GS}{G+S} < G

The ammeter goes in series with the component, and an ideal ammeter has zero resistance so that it does not change the current it is measuring.

As a voltmeter — a high resistance (multiplier) in series. The multiplier takes the excess voltage:

R = \frac{V}{I_g} - G, \qquad R_V = G + R \gg G

The voltmeter goes in parallel with the component, and an ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance so that it draws no current.

Ammeter Voltmeter
Added element shunt S, in parallel multiplier R, in series
Formula S = I_gG/(I-I_g) R = V/I_g - G
Resulting resistance smaller than G larger than G
Connected in series in parallel
Ideal resistance zero infinite
Worked example 14.5 — the same galvanometer, twice

Problem. A galvanometer of resistance 50 Ω gives full-scale deflection at 1 mA.(a) What shunt makes it an ammeter reading 0–1 A?(b) What series resistance makes it a voltmeter reading 0–10 V?

Solution.(a) S = \dfrac{I_gG}{I-I_g} = \dfrac{(10^{-3})(50)}{1-10^{-3}} = 0.050 Ω.(b) R = \dfrac{V}{I_g} - G = \dfrac{10}{10^{-3}} - 50 = 10000 - 50 = 9950 Ω. Note how extreme the two answers are: a shunt of a few hundredths of an ohm, a multiplier of nearly ten thousand ohms.

Series or parallel?

An ammeter in parallel would short-circuit the component and probably burn out; a voltmeter in series would add a huge resistance and stop the current.

If a question says "the meter reads almost zero" or "the lamp goes out", suspect the wrong connection.

And an ammeter of finite resistance always reads slightly less than the true current; a voltmeter of finite resistance always reads slightly less than the true pd.

14.4 Seebeck and Peltier effects; the thermocouple

14.4.1 The Seebeck effect

Join two wires of different metals at both ends and keep the two junctions at different temperatures. A small emf appears in the circuit and a current flows. This is the Seebeck effect, and the pair of wires is a thermocouple. The emf is typically a few millivolts.

  • The emf depends on the pair of metals and on the temperature difference.
  • The greater the separation of the two metals in the thermoelectric series, the larger the emf. Antimony–bismuth gives one of the largest; copper–iron (or copper–constantan) is common in the laboratory.
  • The Seebeck coefficient is \alpha = dE/dT, in V K⁻¹.
  • Reversing the temperature difference reverses the emf; so does interchanging the metals.

A rough thermoelectric series, from one end to the other:

Sb — Fe — Zn — Cu — Ag — Pb — Al — Pt — Ni — Bi

14.4.2 Neutral temperature and temperature of inversion

Keep the cold junction at \theta_c and raise the hot junction to \theta_h. The emf rises, reaches a maximum, then falls, becomes zero, and reverses. Writing E = a\theta + b\theta^2 with \theta = \theta_h - \theta_c:

Point Meaning
Neutral temperature \theta_n the hot-junction temperature at which the emf is maximum (dE/d\theta = 0)
Temperature of inversion \theta_i the hot-junction temperature at which the emf is again zero and then reverses

\theta_i = 2\theta_n - \theta_c

\theta_n is a property of the pair of metals and is practically independent of the cold junction. \theta_i depends on the cold junction: raising \theta_c by 1\,^{\circ}C lowers \theta_i by 1\,^{\circ}C, since \theta_i = 2\theta_n - \theta_c.

Three thermocouple numbers, three different things

\theta_c is the cold junction, \theta_n the temperature of maximum emf, \theta_i the temperature of zero emf. The commonest error is to call \theta_i the maximum, or to forget the factor 2 in \theta_i = 2\theta_n - \theta_c.

Check the arithmetic if \theta_c = 20 °C and \theta_n = 280 °C, then \theta_i = 540 °C, not 560 °C.

Worked example 14.6 — inversion temperature

Problem. A copper–constantan thermocouple has its cold junction at 30 °C and a neutral temperature of 250 °C. At what hot-junction temperature does the emf fall to zero?

Solution. \theta_i = 2\theta_n - \theta_c = 2(250) - 30 = 470 °C.

14.4.3 The Peltier effect

The Peltier effect is the reverse of Seebeck's: send a current through the junction of two dissimilar metals and the junction either absorbs or releases heat. Reverse the current and the effect reverses. The heat is proportional to the charge passed:

H_{Peltier} = \pi I t

where \pi is the Peltier coefficient, the heat absorbed at the junction per unit charge.

Effect Cause How the heat depends on current Reversible?
Seebeck temperature difference produces an emf — yes
Peltier current through a junction produces or absorbs heat \propto I yes
Joule current through a resistance produces heat \propto I^2 no
Thomson current along a wire with a temperature gradient produces or absorbs heat \propto I yes

Because Peltier heat changes sign with the current but Joule heat does not, the two can be separated experimentally.

14.4.4 The thermocouple as a thermometer, and its uses

A thermocouple thermometer has a junction so small that it measures the temperature of a point almost without disturbing it, responds quickly, works over a very wide range (from below 0 °C to over 1000 °C) and needs no power supply.

Its disadvantages are a small emf (needing a sensitive galvanometer or a cold-junction compensation circuit) and the need to keep the reference junction at a known temperature.

  • Thermoelectric generator — a temperature difference drives a current directly, with no moving parts; used in remote places and in radioisotope generators.
  • Peltier cooler — a current cools one junction; used in small refrigerators, cooled CCD cameras and electronic component cooling.
  • Industrial thermometry — thermocouples in furnaces, kilns and engines.

Chapter summary

  • Current is the rate of flow of charge; I = nAev_d with a drift speed of only about 10^{-4} m s⁻¹, while the field that drives it travels at nearly light speed.
  • Ohm's law V = IR holds for metals at constant temperature; R = \rho L/A, and \rho = m/(ne^2\tau) is a property of the material, unchanged by cutting or bending.
  • Metals have \alpha > 0 (about 4\times10^{-3} K⁻¹), semiconductors \alpha < 0, and alloys such as manganin \alpha \approx 0, which is why they make standard resistors.
  • A real cell gives V = E - Ir; the V–I graph has intercept E and slope -r, and the terminal voltage exceeds the emf only while the cell is being charged.
  • P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R; use I^2R in series and V^2/R in parallel; 1 kWh = 3.6\times10^6 J, and the bill is (power in kW) × (hours) × (rate).
  • Series adds resistances and shares the current; parallel adds conductances and shares the voltage. Cells in series raise the emf, in parallel lower the internal resistance, and mixed rows do both with I = nE/(R + nr/m).
  • Kirchhoff: charge is conserved at a junction, energy round a loop. Fix a sign convention, solve, and check the power balance.
  • Wheatstone balance P/Q = R/S; metre bridge R = Sl/(100-l), most accurate with the balance near the middle; potentiometer E \propto l, a null method that draws no current and so measures emf rather than terminal pd.
  • A shunt in parallel makes an ammeter (S = I_gG/(I-I_g), ideal resistance zero); a multiplier in series makes a voltmeter (R = V/I_g - G, ideal resistance infinite).
  • Seebeck: a temperature difference between two junctions of dissimilar metals gives an emf. Peltier: a current through such a junction absorbs or releases heat. The emf peaks at the neutral temperature \theta_n and vanishes at \theta_i = 2\theta_n - \theta_c.

Practice questions

  2. Ohm's law is obeyed whenathe conductor is heatedbthe current is alternatingcthe temperature stays constantdthe conductor is a semiconductor

Group D — Model answers for long questions (10 marks each, for deeper revision)

  1. Derive the relation between current and drift velocity, state Ohm's law and Kirchhoff's laws, and solve circuit numericals. [10]

Model answer D1: drift velocity, Ohm's law and Kirchhoff's laws (10 marks)

Introduction. Electric current is the rate of flow of charge, I = dQ/dt. In a metal it is carried by free electrons that drift slowly under an electric field.

Drift velocity. Let n be the number of free electrons per unit volume in a conductor of area A. In time \Delta t the electrons that cross a section are those within a length v_d\Delta t, so \Delta Q = neAv_d\Delta t and

I = neAv_d, \qquad v_d = \frac{eE\tau}{m}

where \tau is the relaxation time (the average time between collisions). The drift speed is tiny, about 10^{-4}\ \text{m s}^{-1}, yet a lamp lights at once because the field is set up through the wire at nearly the speed of light.

Ohm's law. At constant temperature V = IR. In microscopic form \vec J = \sigma\vec E and \rho = \dfrac{m}{ne^2\tau}, and R = \rho l/A. Resistivity of a metal rises with temperature, R_t = R_0(1 + \alpha t), while for a semiconductor it falls.

Kirchhoff's laws.

  1. Junction law (KCL). The algebraic sum of currents at a junction is zero, which is conservation of charge.
  2. Loop law (KVL). The algebraic sum of emfs and potential drops in a closed loop is zero, which is conservation of energy.
Combination Resistance Current / voltage
Series R = R_1 + R_2 same current
Parallel \dfrac1R = \dfrac1{R_1} + \dfrac1{R_2} same voltage
Cell with internal resistance V = E - Ir I = \dfrac{E}{R + r}

Wheatstone bridge. It is balanced when \dfrac PQ = \dfrac RS, and then no current flows through the galvanometer.

Numerical.

  • A copper wire of cross-section 1\ \text{mm}^2 carries 2\ \text{A} (n = 8.5\times10^{28}\ \text{m}^{-3}): v_d = \dfrac{2}{8.5\times10^{28}\times1.6\times10^{-19}\times10^{-6}} = 1.5\times10^{-4}\ \text{m s}^{-1}.
  • A cell of 12\ \text{V} and 1\ \Omega drives a 5\ \Omega resistor: I = 12/6 = 2\ \text{A} and the terminal voltage is 12 - 2 = 10\ \text{V}.
  • A balanced bridge with P = 10\ \Omega, Q = 20\ \Omega, R = 30\ \Omega has S = 60\ \Omega.

Conclusion. I = neAv_d links the microscopic and macroscopic view of current, and Kirchhoff's two laws solve any network.

Model answer D2: thermoelectric effects (10 marks)

Introduction. Thermoelectricity links temperature differences and electric potential differences.

Seebeck effect. When the two junctions of a loop of two different metals are held at different temperatures, an emf (and a current) appears. It is the basis of the thermocouple (for example copper-constantan or iron-constantan).

For a small temperature difference, E = \alpha\theta + \tfrac12\beta\theta^2, where \theta is measured from the cold junction. The thermoelectric series (Sb, Fe, Cu, ... Bi) tells the direction of the current.

Thermoelectric curve. The emf rises to a maximum at the neutral temperature \theta_n = -\alpha/\beta and then falls to zero at the temperature of inversion \theta_i = 2\theta_n (if the cold junction is 0^{\circ}\text{C}).

For \theta_i = 2\theta_n - \theta_{cold} in general. The neutral temperature does not depend on the cold-junction temperature.

Peltier effect. When a current passes through a junction of two metals, heat is absorbed or liberated, depending on the direction of the current. It is reversible, unlike the Joule heating I^2R, and it is used in small thermoelectric coolers.

Thomson effect. When a current flows in a conductor with a temperature gradient, heat is absorbed or liberated all along the wire, in addition to Joule heating.

Effect What happens Reversible?
Seebeck temperature difference gives emf —
Peltier current gives heating or cooling at a junction yes
Thomson current in a temperature gradient gives heat exchange along the wire yes
Joule heat I^2Rt no

Uses. Thermocouples measure high temperatures in furnaces and engines, thermopiles detect infrared radiation, and thermoelectric generators power space probes.

Numerical. For a thermocouple with \alpha = 16\ \mu\text{V}\,{}^{\circ}\text{C}^{-1} and \beta = -0.04\ \mu\text{V}\,{}^{\circ}\text{C}^{-2}, the neutral temperature is \theta_n = -\dfrac{16}{-0.04} = 400^{\circ}\text{C} and the inversion temperature is 800^{\circ}\text{C} for the cold junction at 0^{\circ}\text{C}.

The maximum emf is 16(400) - 0.02(400)^2 = 6400 - 3200 = 3200\ \mu\text{V} = 3.2\ \text{mV}.

Conclusion. The Seebeck emf rises, peaks at \theta_n and then reverses at \theta_i = 2\theta_n. The Peltier and Thomson effects are reversible heat exchanges.
